name: Aaron Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Northfield, which is a big outfit: six hundred dairy cows on robotic milkers, and about fifteen hundred acres of wheat, maize and grass. The robots do the milking, so my day is more like managing a factory with feelings. I check the overnight alerts on the tablet, chase down cows that haven't visited the robot, clean the units, scrape, and then help on the arable side, which this autumn meant drilling wheat with a GPS-guided tractor. I'm the newest of eight, and the herd manager, Kasia, still has to tell me when a cow just looks wrong. The screen tells me numbers; she sees the animal.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get into farming?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fifteen years on an IT helpdesk for an insurance firm. Resetting passwords, mostly. I got to forty-two, looked out of the window at the car park and thought, I can't do another fifteen. I'd grown up near farms and did a farm skills course at night, and Northfield liked that I wasn't scared of the software. My wife Mette does bookkeeping for small businesses in town, and we've got Freya, thirteen, and Oskar, ten. I use AI every day; I've got it reading the herd data with me and I just got my drone licence for crop spraying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, the hype was overcooked, and I'd post a bit of a told-you-so about the people who said everything would be automated by now. At work I'd say the robots we've got are good enough. Northfield's already as automated as it needs to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Personally, it's good for me. I left IT to get away from screens, and I've ended up somewhere that uses a fair few, but the cows still need people. If AI stalls, I've got a long time to get good at this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Get my drone spraying hours up so I can be the farm's drone person, and do the herd health course in the spring. Keep putting about one-fifty a month aside. Keep using AI for the boring parts, like summarising the vet's reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly smug, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're already on a farm with robots. What's that like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Northfield's got its milking robots, but they still break, cows still get mastitis, gates still get left open. The robot milks the cow perfectly and then a heifer walks through a fence because Oskar's football got stuck in it. Real life is messy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mette's work, a bit. Bookkeeping's exactly the kind of thing even hype-level AI eats into. If her clients use a cheap app instead, our income dips. That would worry me more than anything on the farm.

S0.say: He'd say the hype was overcooked and post a bit of a told-you-so. At work he'd say the farm is already as automated as it needs to be.
S0.think: It's good for him: he left IT for work where cows still need people, and a stall in AI gives him time to get good at farming.
S0.do: Carries on, building drone spraying hours to become the farm's drone person and doing a herd health course in spring. Saves about one-fifty a month and keeps using AI to summarise vet reports.
S0.feel: Calm and, he admits, slightly smug.
S0.quote: The robot milks the cow perfectly and then a heifer walks through a fence because Oskar's football got stuck in it.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron works on a farm that's already heavily automated, so he sees robots as ordinary and messy rather than frightening. Even in the mildest picture his worry turns to his wife's bookkeeping work, which is exposed to thinking AI. He's a daily AI user with the honesty to admit he's smug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance as long as you move early. I'd post about the drone stuff and the herd software, and help people in the farm forum set things up. I'd say to the older lads at Northfield, let me show you, it's not as bad as you think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be in a good spot. The farm would buy more kit, and I'm the one who can set it up and talk to the suppliers. The worry is the same as before: Mette's clients drifting to apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch Kasia on a drone for herd checks and field scouting, and offer to run it. I'd do a short course on farm data, the ag college does one online. And I'd help Mette move her business towards advice, not just data entry, maybe sitting down with her clients over their numbers rather than typing them in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit buzzing. It's the kind of change I left IT to find, weirdly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Northfield might struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Dave, who's done the tractor work for thirty years and hates the GPS. He's not stupid, he just doesn't trust it. I'd offer to teach Dave the GPS if he teaches me how to read a field by walking it. Seems a fair swap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're the newest. Aren't you the one who'd be cut if the farm needs fewer people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not that worried. On a big farm with eight of us, the machines make work as well as take it, at least for a while. Kasia always says the robots made the job different, not smaller.

S1.say: He'd call it a chance for those who move early and help others in the farm forum set up tools. He'd offer to show the older workers the new kit.
S1.think: He thinks he'd be in a good spot as the person who can set up kit and talk to suppliers. His worry is his wife's clients drifting to apps.
S1.do: Pitches the herd manager on a drone for herd checks and field scouting and offers to run it. Takes an online farm data course and helps his wife shift her bookkeeping business towards advice.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit buzzing; it's the kind of change he left IT to find.
S1.quote: I'd offer to teach Dave the GPS if he teaches me how to read a field by walking it. Seems a fair swap.
S1.fieldNote: Aaron sees steady change as an opportunity he's well placed for, and his ideas are practical rather than grand. His offer to swap GPS lessons with an older colleague for field-reading lessons was generous and specific. His blind spot, being the newest hire, didn't worry him much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the faster pictures. The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, adapt or get flattened, which is what I always say. But I'd probably say it with less of a grin. I'd want the government to sort out income support quickly, and I'm not usually the one asking for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's bad for us. If AI can do almost anything, Mette's bookkeeping goes in months, and Northfield's already a robot farm, so they'd need maybe two people where there's eight. I'm the newest. Both incomes, gone inside a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd pay off the car loan with savings and stop putting money into the pension for a bit, keep it liquid. I'd try to sell my drone and data skills to smaller farms that are scrambling to automate, for as long as that's worth paying for. Mette and I would sit down that first week and work out how long four months of savings really lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm usually the calm one, and I wouldn't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've always moved early. Why doesn't that help here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the thing. My whole plan was to be the guy who's good with the robots. If the robots don't need a guy, I haven't got a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Freya and Oskar the truth, gently. That Mum and Dad are working it out, that we've got some savings. Freya would ask me straight if we'll lose the house. She asks everything straight.

S2.say: He'd say 'adapt or get flattened', but with less of a grin, and want the government to sort out income support quickly, which isn't usually his line.
S2.think: He thinks both his and his wife's incomes would go within a year: her bookkeeping in months, and his job on a farm already run by robots.
S2.do: Pays off the car loan and pauses pension contributions to keep cash available. Sells drone and data skills to smaller farms scrambling to automate, and works out with his wife how long four months of savings really lasts.
S2.feel: Alarmed; he's usually the calm one and wouldn't be.
S2.quote: My whole plan was to be the guy who's good with the robots. If the robots don't need a guy, I haven't got a plan.
S2.fieldNote: Aaron's whole strategy is to be good with the robots, and fast AGI removes that. With both incomes exposed, his adaptability doesn't save him and he says so plainly. He's a centrist who'd find himself asking for government help, which surprised him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it, if you're willing to change. I'd be posting guides for small farms on how to set up kit cheaply. And I'd say the government should help with the cost of training, not just leave it to the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I think I'd do alright for most of it. Small farms would be buying kit and need someone to set it up. Then by year five the kit sets itself up, and I'd need the next thing. I'd be forty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd start a small farm-tech setup business on my days off, drones, sensors, robot milkers, charging maybe sixty an hour. Mette would do the books, while there's still books to do. We'd put most of what it earns into savings, and maybe buy a few shares in the companies making the robots, as a hedge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Busy and uneasy, which is better than idle and uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be helping the robots replace farm workers. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the gamble. I'd spend five years helping farms need fewer people, knowing one of the people they won't need is me. At least I'd have savings from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you know it's time to switch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably in year three, the moment I saw the robots fixing each other. That's when I'd stop building the setup business and start looking at what's left that people want from people.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it if you're willing to change, and post guides for small farms on setting up kit cheaply. He'd want government help with training costs.
S3.think: He thinks he'd do alright for most of the five years setting up kit for small farms, then need something new at 48.
S3.do: Starts a farm-tech setup business on days off, charging about sixty an hour for drones, sensors and milking robots, with his wife doing the books. Saves most of the earnings and buys a few shares in robot makers as a hedge.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy, which he finds better than idle and uneasy.
S3.quote: I'd spend five years helping farms need fewer people, knowing one of the people they won't need is me.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Aaron profit from the transition, and he's frank that he'd be helping farms need fewer people, including himself. He has a clear trigger for switching: seeing robots fix each other. Buying shares in the robot makers is his hedge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a proper runway. I'd tell people at Northfield and in the forum to use it, learn something, save something. And I'd be making the case for sensible help, but not for stopping it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be fifty-three, Freya out of school, Oskar nearly. The mortgage would be close to done. I think I'd come out alright, though I don't really know what the work looks like at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at Northfield and get really good with the herd for the first few years, and run the setup business on the side. I'd put a bit more each month into those robot-maker shares. And I'd start looking at something with people in it for the long run, maybe teaching farm skills at the college where I did my evening course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but the healthy kind. Like before a big exam you've revised for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you don't know what the work looks like at the end. Doesn't that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the honest answer. I'm good at moving, but moving needs somewhere to move to. If a robot can do anything, ten years only helps if I spend it getting good at being a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mette say about your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mette would say I should spend more time at home, honestly. I've been working seven days since the farm job started. Maybe that's the thing to protect, whatever happens.

S4.say: He'd call ten years a proper runway and tell people to learn and save. He'd argue for sensible help but not for stopping the change.
S4.think: At 53, with children nearly grown and the mortgage close to done, he thinks he'd come out alright, though he doesn't know what work will look like at the end.
S4.do: Stays at the dairy farm for a few years while running the setup business on the side and adding to robot-maker shares each month. Starts looking at people-centred work for the long run, such as teaching farm skills at the local college.
S4.feel: Uneasy in a healthy way, like before an exam he has revised for.
S4.quote: If a robot can do anything, ten years only helps if I spend it getting good at being a person.
S4.fieldNote: Even with a decade, Aaron admits his adaptability needs somewhere to go. His thought about getting good at being a person shifts his focus from tech skills to teaching and family. His wife's view that he works too much came up unprompted.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I've built everything on being good with the machines, and in two years the machines don't need me, and they don't need Mette either. What would help is some income to fall back on while we retrain, and cheap training for the jobs that are left, which I suspect are the ones with people in them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the cows, maybe. People think a robot farm is cold. The cows at Northfield actually seem calmer since the robots came, because nobody's rushing them in at five in the morning. I don't know what that says about us.

headlineQuote: The cows at Northfield actually seem calmer since the robots came, because nobody's rushing them in at five in the morning.
portrait: Aaron Jensen is 43, the newest of eight workers on a large dairy and arable farm that already milks with robots. He left fifteen years of IT helpdesk work to be outdoors, uses AI every day and has a drone licence. In the milder pictures he's calm and keen to be the farm's tech person. Fast AGI alarms him because both his job and his wife's bookkeeping would go within a year, and his plan of being good with robots stops working. With 5 or 10 years he'd run a farm-tech side business, invest in robot makers and look towards teaching and work with people.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he has built everything on being good with machines, and in two years neither he nor his wife would be needed.
whatWouldHelp: Income to fall back on while retraining, and cheap training for the jobs that remain, which he expects to be the ones involving people.
